Based on the provided healthcare Q&A matches, here is a synthesized answer to the user's question:

When considering first-line treatment for high-risk metastatic breast cancer patients, some questions arise about whether single-agent mitoxantrone (a type of chemotherapy drug) is as effective as combination chemotherapy. In response, several studies have investigated this.

One study found that while there was no significant difference in response or survival between mitoxantrone and low-dose fluorocitrate (FEC) when used alone in high-risk metastatic breast cancer patients, the toxicities associated with mitoxantrone favored the single-agent treatment. This suggests that quality of life may be more important than potential prolongation of survival for some patients.

Another study suggested that Ki-67, a marker of cell proliferation, can predict response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy in breast cancer patients. However, this predictive ability is most pronounced for the molecular subtype of the tumor.

Regarding immediate breast reconstruction after chemotherapy, research has found no evidence to suggest that it compromises the delivery of adjuvant (chemotherapy) treatment. While there was a notable incidence of implant infection, which could be related to other factors, this finding doesn't necessarily imply a negative impact on chemotherapy efficacy.

Additionally, studies have explored the potential benefits of combining mitoxantrone with 2-methoxyestradiol (2ME), an estradiol metabolite, in treating hormone-dependent cancer. The findings suggest that this combination may offer a new treatment regimen with enhanced antiproliferative activity and improved tolerability.

Lastly, concerning breast cancer survival rates, research indicates that the prognosis for patients with recurrent breast cancer has shown improvement between 1974 and 2000.

In conclusion, while there are questions surrounding first-line single-agent mitoxantrone in high-risk metastatic breast cancer treatment, multiple studies provide insight into these issues. The available evidence suggests that quality of life may be more important than survival benefits for some patients, while combination chemotherapy with 2ME has shown promise in hormone-dependent cancers and improved tolerability compared to mitoxantrone alone. Further research is necessary to fully understand the implications of these findings.
